q: Why do two carbon reports for the same factory and year show different totals?
title: Why two carbon reports disagree
short: Two reports for the same factory and year usually differ because they drew different boundaries, used different factor versions, chose different Scope 3 methods, or counted different gases. Line them up by scope, then by source, and the gap almost always traces to three or four lines.
audience: MSMEs comparing a consultant's figure with a software or buyer estimate

ol: Scope 3 method: one report multiplies tonnes of material by a material factor, the other multiplies rupee spend by an economic factor. This alone can move Scope 3 by a large share.
Scope 3 coverage: one report includes only purchased goods, the other adds freight, waste and business travel.
Boundary: one includes a leased warehouse, a second plant or contractor diesel used on site; the other does not.
Factor versions: different editions of the CEA grid database, or an international grid factor in place of the Indian one.
Scope 2 basis: location-based in one, market-based with RECs or a green tariff in the other.
Gases and GWP: CO2 only for fuels in one, CO2e with refrigerant leaks at AR5 or AR6 values in the other.
Period: April to March in one, January to December in the other.

sections.h: How to find the gap in an afternoon
ol: Put both reports side by side and compare Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3 separately. The gap usually sits in one scope.
Within that scope, compare activity quantities first: litres, kWh, tonnes. If quantities differ, it is a boundary or data issue.
If quantities match, compare factors and their sources. If factors differ, it is a method or version issue.
Ask both preparers for the line items behind the scope that differs.

p: Neither is right by default. Use the one whose boundary matches what you were asked for, whose factors are named and current, and whose quantities trace to documents. If a buyer prescribes a method or factor set, use that and keep the other report's working as a reconciliation note.

sections.h: How this differs from a Scope 3 tool gap
p: When only the Scope 3 figures differ, the cause is nearly always method and category mapping. When Scope 1 or 2 differ too, look first at boundary and factor versions, because the underlying fuel and electricity quantities should be the same in both reports.

example.title: Illustrative example: one factory, two reports, a 28% gap
lines: Diesel in both: 20,000 L x 2.68 kg CO2/L = 53.6 t CO2
Report A electricity: 300,000 kWh x 0.710 (CEA v21.0) = 213.0 t CO2
Report B electricity: 300,000 kWh x 0.80 (assumed older factor, illustrative) = 240.0 t CO2
Report A steel: 200 t x 2.0 t CO2e/t (assumed material factor) = 400 t CO2e
Report B steel: Rs 1.6 crore x 0.035 kg CO2e per rupee (assumed spend factor) = 560 t CO2e
Gap: 187.0 t, so Report B is about 28% higher; the steel method causes 160 t of it
example.note: The 0.80 grid factor, the steel factor and the spend factor are assumptions chosen to show the mechanics, not published values.

senseible: Senseible pins the factor and its source to each line, which lets you compare its figures with another report line by line. Spend-based Scope 3 estimates are labelled as spend-based with wider uncertainty, so they are not mistaken for activity-based figures.
